paper_title: X-Tree: Tokenizing Reusable Experience for Efficient Agent Generalization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-step agents are trained on flat action streams: SFT and RLVR weight every token uniformly and ignore the sub-procedures that recur across tasks, the hierarchy that lets humans plan top-down from reusable routines. This structure sits unused, and flat training uses each scarce trajectory less fully than its content allows. Recent agents do use that structure, but only as LLM-written skills in context, never in the weights, so their gains do not generalize beyond retrieval. We instead recover this hierarchy from the data itself and train on it, with no LLM calls. Following text tokenizers, which build a vocabulary by counting alone, we score action spans by reusability and merge canonicalized actions into a reusable eXperience tree (X-Tree). Each X-Tree node captures how a frequent and success-bearing skill is composed from sub-skills, guiding efficient generalization. We integrate X-Tree into three training settings: offline RL, with each node as a training instance; online RLVR, with an adaptive skill bonus; and on-policy self-distillation, with X-Tree as the self-teacher's privileged context. Across WebArena, ScienceWorld, and WebShop at three model scales, X-Tree improves over standard recipes at matched data and budget by up to 4.5% SR on WebArena, 5.8% SR on ScienceWorld and 4.1% success on WebShop. Matched analyses attribute the gains to the X-Tree structure and the three integrations.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Human learners spontaneously discover hierarchies that compose recurring action sequences, acting from goals through sub-goals to primitives (Miller, 1956; Botvinick et al., 2009). Language models trained to operate websites (Zhou et al., 2023), resolve repository issues (Jimenez et al., 2024), and act over long-horizon interactive environments (Xie et al., 2024; Xi et al., 2024) learn the opposite way. trajectory enters training, whether SFT or RLVR, as flat stream of actions, and the objective weights every token equally (Ouyang et al., 2022; Shao et al., 2024). This equal weighting overlooks the sub-procedures that recur across tasks, such as browse-and-select or pick-up-and-move. The hierarchy is present in the data, but the training objective does not use it. Uniform training therefore extracts less from each trajectory than the data allows, requiring more data to learn. This underutilization is especially costly because experience is scarce. trajectory is collected by human (Wang et al., 2025) or synthesized and verified by model (Gandhi & Neubig, 2025). An environment must be built, its tasks written, and its verifier made trustworthy. None of this scales the way web text does. We therefore ask how to extract the most from finite set of experience. To extract more insight from given pool of experience, recent agent harnesses such as OpenClaw ask an LLM to summarize past experience as natural-language workflows and replay them in context (Wang et al., 2023; 2024). Nothing is compressed into the weights, so the experience cannot generalize beyond retrieval. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead brings such skills into training, where self-teacher reads them as privileged context and re-weights the learners own tokens (Zhao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Both depend on an LLM to write the abstraction, which is costly, uncontrollable and leaves library which cannot be reproduced from the data alone.

We train X-Tree into model weights by integrating X-Tree as data (offline RL), as reward (online RLVR) and as context (OPSD). Figure 5 demonstrates concrete X-Tree example from trajectory. Language models already solve the analogous problem for text before learning begins. recurrencebased tokenizer merges co-occurring characters into structured vocabulary (Sennrich et al., 2016). In this paper, we tokenize experience into reusable structures (Figure 1). We canonicalize each action step in trajectory into typed token (i.e., verb<role>). We introduce -Score, measure of reusability that scores span by how often it recurs, how long it is, and how often it appears in successful episodes. Guided by -Score, we merge adjacent pairs into nodes, then merge nodes into larger nodes hierarchically. This produces reusable eXperience tree (X-Tree), deterministic, auditable hierarchy over trajectory corpus built with zero LLM calls. Each X-Tree node captures how frequent and success-bearing skill is composed from sub-skills, guiding efficient generalization. Our preliminary result shows that X-Tree is already useful as in-context advice (Appendix C). We integrate X-Tree into three training settings (Figure 2). 1) Offline RL, when only trajectories exist without an environment. Each X-Tree node acts as one training instance. The policy partially rolls out from the gold prefix that precedes the node. We optimize with GRPO over step-matching reward with depth scaled completion bonus. 2) Online RLVR, when an environment and verifier exist. X-Tree adds bonus for each X-Tree skill rollout executes with an adaptive weight that supplies signal while verifier signal is scarce and down-weights it as the signal becomes informative. 3) OPSD, where X-Tree replaces the LLM-written skill bank that the self-teacher reads. We experiment across three environments and three model scales at matched data and budget. Our offline RL with X-Tree gains 4.5% success rate (SR) over full-data SFT on WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023) with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablations, such as random tree, attribute the gain to X-Tree and our RL method. Our online RLVR with X-Tree stays ahead of outcome-based RL across all scales by up to 4.9% SR, leading the held-out tasks, on ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022). It also consistently outperforms standard recipe by up to 3.6% success and 4.6% graded score on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022). For OPSD, X-Tree as the privileged context of self-teacher matches LLM-written skills, with no LLM calls on both ScienceWorld and WebShop at all scales. We summarize our contributions: X-Tree, which tokenizes reusable experience from trajectory pool into deterministic hierarchy of skills with zero LLM calls. Each node captures the compositional signals to guide training. Three integrations of X-Tree with training, as data, reward, and context: offline RL for the trajectories-only setting; online RLVR with an adaptive, verifier-aligned skill bonus; and OPSD with X-Tree as the self-teachers privileged context (3.23.4). Experiments across three environments and three scales showing that X-Tree improves over standard recipes at matched data and budget by large margin, with ablations that attribute gains to X-Tree structure and to the three integrations (5).

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Hierarchy learning. Hierarchical organization of behavior is an established finding in cognitive science: capacity limits force recoding into reusable structures, and learners act from goals through sub-goals to primitives (Miller, 1956; Gobet et al., 2001; Botvinick et al., 2009), choosing decompositions that trade utility against planning cost (Solway et al., 2014; Correa et al., 2023). long line of work recovers such structure from demonstrations by segmenting trajectories into options or sub-policies (Sutton et al., 1999; Konidaris et al., 2012; Fox et al., 2017; Shiarlis et al., 2018; Kipf et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2022). We take from it the finding that bottom-up training on flat action streams overlooks structure learner should exploit. We recover the hierarchy as tree structure over actions handed to training rather than as set of advice in context. LLM-induced skills and experience reuse. Recent agents ask proprietary model to summarize reusable experience as natural-language workflows (Wang et al., 2023; 2024; Tang et al., 2025) or executable tools (Zheng et al., 2025; Prabhu et al., 2025), or store raw experience as verbal reflections, distilled insights and retrieved trajectories (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024a; Su et al., 2025). Both families keep the skills in prompt or tool registry, costing LLM calls for abstraction. Skills are never compressed into the model, not generalizing beyond retrieval. We replace the abstraction step with deterministic miner and train the skills into the weights. Compression as abstraction. Grammar induction over symbol sequences (Nevill-Manning & Witten, 1997) and dictionary compression (Larsson & Moffat, 2000) are the classical ancestors. Library learning compresses programs under description-length objective (Ellis et al., 2021; Bowers et al., 2023; Grand et al., 2024). And robot policies tokenize continuous actions by vector quantization (Lee et al., 2024). Closest to us, PRISE (Zheng et al., 2024b) and Subwords-as-Skills (Yunis et al., 2023) apply Byte-Pair-Encoding (BPE) to quantized continuous-control actions. We differ in alphabet (typed actions from canonicalizer), in merge criterion (X -Score to measure reusability, as behavior carries more information than text), and in the use of vocabulary: not fixed macro-action space but reusable experience as prior to guide training as data, as credit and as context. Multi-turn agent training. Many domains lack an online environment and task verifier (Zhou et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024). Our offline RL integration with X-Tree provides solution to train from the trajectory data Gandhi & Neubig (2025) alone. Recent studies train agents online with multi-turn RL (Qi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) using policy-gradient (Feng et al., 2025). Unlike learned process-reward model, our shaping signal is mined from the trajectory pool itself. On the other hand, on-policy self-distillation trains model toward its own predictions under privileged context (Zhao et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). We keep that objective and replace the LLM-written privileged context with the X-Tree.

sections.content: Offline RL: WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023). We mine 256 X-Tree skills from 7.9k trajectories (Gandhi & Neubig, 2025). We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with SFT on half the pool, then one GRPO stage on X-Tree nodes from the other half by verl. Appendix lists training details. Evaluation runs the 694 deterministic (non-fuzzy) tasks, 30-step cap with official reward. We evaluate success rate (SR) with normalization, i.e., task counts as success if the official evaluator returns 1, or, for the exact match tasks, if the normalized gold string appears verbatim in the final output. All baselines are based on the same harness. Appendix shows more details. Online RLVR: ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022) and WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), three scales. We use SFT warm starts from 200 (ScienceWorld) and 500 (WebShop) trajectories at 1.5B/3B/7B, then GRPO stage. sections.title: 5 RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: We validate the three training integrations (3) over three environments and three model scales. We show the main result first and then the ablations that isolate where its gain comes from. 5.1 OFFLINE RL ON WEBARENA X-Tree turns fixed trajectory pool into +4.5 SR without any other information. With the same trajectories and no environment at training, offline RL with X-Tree reaches 24% relative gain over Go-Browse recipe (SFT-Full) (Table 1, 22.9 vs 18.4). Matching RL compute with two extra SFT epochs raises SFT-Full by only 0.4, so the gain is not from compute. Our offline RL approach reliably boosts SFT performance, and adding X-Tree leads to further gains. This validates both our RL method and X-Tree structure, significantly improving the multi-turn agent learning under the same budget. Our improvement is consistent across all sites, with especially large margins on the three biggest sites compared to SFT recipe: admin improves the most (+6.4 SR), followed by gitlab, the most procedure-intensive site (+5.2 SR), and then shopping (+4.9 SR). The margin shrinks on reddit, map and wiki, since they are driven mainly by query formulation, not procedural execution. Moreover, the hierarchical reward we propose (3.2) performs better than simply mixing X-Tree nodes with flat reward or depth-based curriculum training. This suggests the presence of reusable structure in trajectory data that merits further investigation. On the same budget, X-Tree captures informative signals that facilitate enhanced compositional generalization in offline RL. Our recipe also transfers to another model family (GLM-4) and larger scale (14B) (Appendix E).

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Limited experience is the current bottleneck in training multi-step agents. Standard recipes consume the action sequence uniformly and bottom-up, without the hierarchy that lets human learners generalize more efficiently with the same data. We tokenize reusable experience to recover that hierarchy from trajectory pool as X-Tree, with zero LLM calls. Each X-Tree node captures how recurrent

XTree enters training in three settings: as the training instance in offline RL, as an adaptive bonus that keeps online RLVR ahead while the outcome signal is scarce, and as the privileged context in OPSD where it matches the LLM-written skill bank. Analyses attribute the gain to the X-Tree structure and our integration design. These results hold across three environments and three model scales. Limitations. We mine X-Tree once from fixed pool, and integrate X-Tree with training without improving it. Mining from the policys own trajectories would potentially let the structure and the policy improve together in loop. We evaluate the three integrations one per setting and never combine them. possible future work is to train single model on X-Tree nodes, taking the X-Tree bonus, and distill from X-Tree at once. X-Tree also only reorganizes experience that already exists. Because it records which pairs recur and which succeed, it marks where corpus is thin, identifying the trajectories worth synthesizing to fill the gap.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 TRAINING DETAILS Tables 6 to 8 show the hyperparameters behind experiments. Table 8 covers the X-Tree in-context evaluation in Appendix C. The offline stage is our node-as-instance offline RL based on verl. ScienceWorld runs with the code of Zhang et al. (2025) with our reward bonus. WebShops RLVR is based on verl-agent Feng et al. (2025), and the OPSD is based on the code of (Lu et al., 2026). Hinted by Table 5, building X-Tree does not need large trajectory pool to help. However, previous studies (Cheng et al., 2025b) show that RL generalization requires decent SFT-built base. Every online run in this paper therefore starts from small warm start: on ScienceWorld and WebShop we sample 200 and 500 trajectories from the trajectory pool. Within every comparison we report, all experiments (including RLVR and OPSD) start from the same warm-start checkpoint for model scale in an environment. A.2 CANONICALIZATION EXAMPLES The purpose is to better recognize reusable structures in the corpus. Tables 9 to 11 show the templates from raw action to canonical token. Properties of the template are three-fold: 1) deterministic: written once per environment from the action space, 2) complete: no action can fail to canonicalize and none is silently dropped, and 3) no loss of information: every trimmed value, e.g., an element id, typed text, an object name, is kept so it could still be used after X-Tree mining. Chain-of-Thought never enters the alphabet. On ScienceWorld the object class c() is an ordered keyword lexicon of nine classes, tried in order: door, instrument, paint, container, device, plant, animal, substance, location, with the literal head noun kept when nothing matches and location the closed list of the ten ScienceWorld rooms. Instance numbers and containment qualifiers are stripped before the match and preserved. This is what makes move thermometer to metal pot and move thermometer to ceramic cup the same symbol, putc(Y ) = putcontainer, while keeping both distinct from move thermometer to stove. Simplified examples in Figure 1 and 2 are for illustration purpose.
